sections.title: Change, causal finitude, and ultimate explanation
Divine attributes, freedom, and the gap problem
Perfect creation, evil, and evolutionary suffering
Moral reality, privation, and human value

moves.speaker: Trent Horn

sourceSpan.excerpt: seven therefore there must be a first actualizer eight this first actualizer could not have any potential and so it must be an unactualized actualizer or that which is pure act since an infinite regress of concurrent causes is impossible the first cause must not rely on anything else to actualize its own potential to exist in that respect it must be pure existence or pure actuality itself moreover this cause could not have any other potentialities because like everything else we observe what the cause does follows from what it is and what it is at its most basic level is existence or actuality itself to say this first actualizer has perfect existence but another part of it doesn't exist or it only exists potentially would be a contradiction nine if something is pure act it would be god ten therefore god exists

moves.inventoryRationale: This is Horn's principal metaphysical route from observed dependent actuality to the motion's affirmative conclusion.

sourceSpan.excerpt: premise m claims god's perfection rules out unjustified evils as imperfections so why believe premise end that claims there are such imperfections as unjustified evils i will argue we can justify premise in using an inductive method and the moral assumption that the world is on the whole imperfect unless all its wrong making properties are sufficiently counterbalanced by right-making properties both known and unknown we'll let n be god's allowance of any seemingly unjustified evil or imperfection are any unknown right-making property and w any unknown wrong-making property such that there are only four possible outcomes for any particular n in three of these four possibilities n is an unjustified evil all things considered because it has wrong making characteristics that are not counter balanced by its right making characteristics so it is three times as likely any particular n is an unjustified evil supposing there may be some right-making and wrong-making properties unknown to us the atheist philosopher michael tooley shows the probability all these evils are actually morally justified to allow all things considered must be less than one over n plus one because n is a very large number the probability it is morally permissible to allow all these evils is extremely small thus we have inductively justified premise end that there are probably some unjustified evils all things considered therefore my conclusion o follows theism is probably false all things considered

sourceSpan.excerpt: naturalism entails the universe is indifferent to the nature and conditions of sentient life using likelihood comparisons i argue there are at least three evolutionary observations about evil that are more likely given naturalism than theism first according to what i'll call the evolutionary languishing of sentient beings for hundreds of millions of years biological organisms have experienced mostly profound languishing predation starvation and disease secondly 99 of all species that have ever lived are now extinct and and the state of nature is locked in a savage struggle for survival over limited resources finally according to personal tragedy some lose themselves entirely by coming to believe their lives are on the whole no longer worth living another interesting point about all these observations is that they are straightforward physical implications of the second law of thermodynamics according to this law of nature entropy or the measure of disorder in the universe is always increasing because there are more ways for things to be disordered than to be ordered there are many more ways for animals to suffer than for them to experience pleasure many ways for life to languish than to flourish and many more ways for us to experience tragedy than triumph naturalism predicts this kind of thermodynamic indifference towards sentient life however given trent's classical theism these are neither accidental nor unfortunate byproducts of an intentionally designed process but are rather the very clockwork of the process itself this is the divine means by which god intentionally chose to bring about the goal of finite creatures through his creative act so god actively employed gratuitous pain languishing and tragedy in his provincial production of humanity for hundreds of millions of years

sourceSpan.excerpt: well thank you ben for that opening statement here are some thoughts we'll talk about low probability ben's definition of naturalism seemed to only be the negation of the supernatural but any specific explanation is going to have a lower intrinsic probability than the mere negation of an explanation for example the intrinsic probability jones killed smith is lower than the negation that anything else killed smith but it doesn't follow that the most probable explanation therefore is that no specific thing killed smith in the same vein we shouldn't follow this reasoning and think the most intrinsically probable explanation for the universe is no specific explanation at all

moves.inventoryRationale: This is Horn's direct reply to the prior-probability framework.

sourceSpan.excerpt: god chose to allow humans to morally develop in a process that creates unique goods and evils so god chose animals to biologically develop so that unique goods and evils would exist uh two the very existence of animals may justify suffering that they endure for example most people wouldn't think it wrong for humans to terraform a planet in the solar system and create sentient life knowing that it will languish also we would be fine to leave the earth and not destroy it if we wanted to go colonize a new planet but if humans can create or allow animal suffering to continue because it is good that animals exist why can't god do the same three if sentient animals have a sense of self enduring sense they might be compensated in the afterlife if they don't have an enduring sense of self over time this makes the problem of their suffering much less pressing uh when it comes to the evil of non-belief in god just as god gives us a long leash when it comes to making moral mistakes even grave ones so that we can have certain goods like free will the theists would say it makes sense that god gives us a long leash to make epistemic mistakes so that certain goods could obtain like freely choosing god but if god can bring greater goods from evil then that evil can be justified and in fact i don't think it'd be obvious everyone believes god exists i think consciousness and free will and temporal becoming are obvious but there's many philosophers who don't believe those things exist so if god were as obvious as those things people still might not believe in him finally probabilistic arguments they're misleading because you've got to have all the background knowledge not just the things that make things less likely but all the stuff that makes it even more likely a 600 pound person is probably not an athlete but if they're a world-class sumo wrestler oh now you've changed all the background knowledge to reach a different conclusion finally

the very existence of animals may justify suffering that they endure

moves.attributionBasis: The locked format identifies this as Horn's first rebuttal.

responseComponents.text: Biological development, animal existence, and possible compensation supply candidate goods connected to animal suffering.
Probabilistic evil arguments are incomplete unless evidence favoring God and possible justifying goods are included in the background information.
Epistemic freedom and freely choosing God are candidate goods for permitting mistaken nonbelief.

moves.proposition: Evolutionary and epistemic suffering may enable distinctive goods or compensation, and likelihood judgments must incorporate all relevant background evidence.
moves.inventoryRationale: This move gathers Horn's linked theodicies and his methodological objection to Watkins's likelihood comparisons.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn

sourceSpan.excerpt: when it comes to free will ben's argument is ambiguous when he says god is devoid of potentialities classical theists agree god has no passive potentiality he can have active potentiality nothing affects god but god can refrain from affecting other things like letting the dinosaurs have another million years premise finally premise w says a will devoid of any contingencies could not have done otherwise this is a fallacy of accident because it compares the divine will to the human will human wills are in time and limited and have to do discursive reasoning god is timeless and all-knowing and does not have to process things in the same way so we would not expect god's will to achieve different results to have any kind of intrinsic contingency so i think

responseComponents.text: Classical theism denies passive potentiality in God but permits active power and restraint.
The inference treats timeless divine willing like temporally deliberative human willing.

moves.proposition: Watkins equivocates between passive and active potentiality and wrongly transfers constraints of temporal human willing to God's timeless will.
moves.inventoryRationale: This directly answers each pivotal link in the freedom argument.

moves.speaker: Ben Watkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: first trent's argument makes a crucial assumption he assumes the existence of some substance at time t presupposes the concurrent actualization of its potential for its existence let's call this the sustaining causation thesis i believe naturalists have no good reason to accept this first we can follow j.h sobel who trent quoted earlier tonight in pointing out that there is no justification for thinking that something is being moved from potential to actual with respect to its existence change is evident to the senses but a concurrent actualization of something's existence is by no means evident to the senses yet the existence of such a per se chain is precisely what trent's argument needs to succeed the thesis of existential inertia can account for all the data that trent appeals to second trent's argument relies on the distinction between essence and existence trent is assuming existence is not an intrinsic feature of a thing's essence a naturalist can simply reject this assumption on the grounds of metaphysical simplicity we can say that one the universe does not contain non-existent essences and two existence can can be an intrinsic feature of all essences this is a simpler model that offers a rebutting defeater to trent's assumption the second objection i want to mention we can call the quantifier shift fallacy even granting trent's assumptions it does not follow that there is a single unique unactualized actualizer just as it does not follow there's a single unique counselor for all students from the fact that for each such student he or she has a counselor it likewise does not follow there's a first cause of all per se chains from the fact that for each such chain it has a single unactualized actualizer even if things have per se efficient causes there is no obvious reasons why all things must have the same first per se efficient cause let's now

quoteEligibleExactSpans: the thesis of existential inertia can account for all the data
existence can can be an intrinsic feature of all essences
we can call the quantifier shift fallacy
moves.attributionBasis: The locked format identifies this as Watkins's first rebuttal.

responseComponents.text: Observed change does not establish concurrent actualization of existence; existential inertia is an alternative account.
Naturalism can deny the assumed real distinction between essence and existence.
A first actualizer for each causal chain does not entail one shared actualizer for every chain.

moves.proposition: Horn's motion argument assumes unproved sustaining causation and essence-existence distinctions and illicitly infers one universal first actualizer.
moves.inventoryRationale: These are Watkins's three distinct but jointly delivered attacks on Horn's central cosmological proof.

moves.speaker: Ben Watkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: according to what i'll call the gap problem neither of these arguments give us any moral information these arguments cannot undercut even in principle and argument from evil and imperfection so long as that argument is still on the table and we have reasons to think those arguments are sound trent's arguments cannot succeed thirdly trent asks is the cause of the universe necessary i doubt this a necessary cause of the universe leads to modal collapse if x is caused by something necessary then that necessary cause entails x however a necessary cause will entail other necessities this leads to modal fatalism and trent's causal phenotypism can't bridge the gap between contingency and necessity trent also asked if the cause of the universe is personal trent rules out a material cause for the universe but all known mental activity has a physical basis in material brains this provides inductive support for the view there are no mental changes without any material changes that claim is an undercutting defeater for inferring a personal mind that is the cause of the universe also consider my prior arguments from hiddenness and evil here finally trent asks if the cause of the universe is good even if we suppose the universe is finite and has a cause the arguments from evil and imperfection are rebutting defeaters for inferring a good cause of the universe again here we see the gap problem

quoteEligibleExactSpans: neither of these arguments give us any moral information
a necessary cause of the universe leads to modal collapse
all known mental activity has a physical basis in material brains
moves.attributionBasis: The locked format identifies this as Watkins's first rebuttal.

responseComponents.text: Cosmological conclusions alone supply no moral information capable of defeating the imperfection evidence.
A necessary cause appears to entail necessary effects and modal fatalism.
Known minds depend on material brains, undercutting the inference to an immaterial personal cause.
Even a finite past does not identify its cause as the personal, good God of classical theism.

moves.proposition: Horn's cosmological results leave an evidential gap to goodness and personality, while necessity risks modal collapse and known mentality is physically dependent.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Watkins's load-bearing gap objection and its specific modal, mental, and moral applications.

moves.speaker: Ben Watkins

quoteEligibleExactSpans: basic moral truths are necessary truths
they are not evidence for either naturalism or theism

distinguish between moral agents and moral patients

responseComponents.text: Necessary moral truths hold under either worldview and therefore do not favor theism.
Irreducibly normative reasons can ground value, wrongness, duties, and the moral-agent distinction without God.

moves.proposition: A secular robust moral realism treats basic moral truths and reasons as necessary and irreducibly normative, explaining value and responsibility without evidential support for theism.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Watkins's developed alternative account rather than a bare denial of Horn's moral case.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn

sourceSpan.excerpt: well let's look at ben's criticisms for my case for the existence of god uh he took aim at the argument from motion that's saying you don't need an actualizer for a thing's continuing existence because things could just have existential inertia well there's tons of problems with this first existential inertia is not well studied it doesn't tell us if an ultimate theory is true rather our ultimate theories tell us whether existential inertia is true or not paul audi and one of the few recent treatments on existential inertia says it would be most likely to exist if change were simply an illusion but the second law of thermodynamics that things tend towards decay and the fact that you can know a thing's essence uh apart from its existence count again counts against the view that objects possess a tendency to exist that doesn't need to be actualized and finally using existential inertia against theism argues in a circle by claiming objects merely have a property of continuing existence and that property exists because of the object whose very existence is invoked to explain it there's a circular relationship between the substance and the property of existential inertia and yeah i would say no existence and essence are distinct because i can talk to my son about the essence of horses unicorns and triceratops but telling him the essence of those things will not tell him horses do exist unicorns never exist and triceratops once existed he

quoteEligibleExactSpans: existential inertia is not well studied
using existential inertia against theism argues in a circle
existence and essence are distinct
moves.attributionBasis: The locked format identifies this as Horn's second rebuttal.

responseComponents.text: Existential inertia is dependent on an antecedent metaphysical theory rather than neutral data.
Explaining an object's continued existence by a property belonging to that object is circular.
Knowing what horses, unicorns, and triceratops are does not disclose whether or when they exist.

moves.proposition: Existential inertia is theory-dependent and circular, while ordinary essence judgments demonstrate that essence and existence are distinct.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Horn's focused answer to Watkins's sustaining-causation and essence objections.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn

responseComponents.text: Horn says his inference rests on the impossibility of infinite causal chains, not the quantified form Watkins attributes to it.

moves.proposition: The causal conclusion follows from excluding infinite chains, not a quantifier shift, and creation ex nihilo produces only an extrinsic change relative to God.
moves.inventoryRationale: The fourth pro cosmological move is retained because it contacts two separate burdens—chain termination and creation-related immutability—that cannot be merged into the existential-inertia reply without obscuring each answer.

responseComponents.text: Calling evil a privation does not explain why a perfect God permits the missing good.
Identifying goodness with being crosses the is-ought divide and reduces goodness claims to trivial existence claims.
Pain and depression appear positively bad, and reasons to avoid them conflict with treating their existing reality as good.

moves.proposition: The privation theory neither explains missing goods nor respects the is-ought distinction and cannot plausibly represent positively agonizing experiences.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: The cosmological section contains four pro moves and one con move because Horn presents separate pure-act and finite-past constructions and later gives distinct replies to existential inertia and finite-chain or creation objections, while Watkins bundles his interrelated cosmological objections into one load-bearing rebuttal. The total 14-to-12 selection preserves those source-distinct burdens without inventing symmetry.

sections.rationale: Horn's fourth row is necessary because his original pure-act proof, finite-past argument, reply to existential inertia and essence-existence denial, and reply concerning finite chains and extrinsic creation contact distinct burdens; merging the two replies would obscure their different targets.

Watkins's fourth row is necessary because the perfect-creator premise, inductive unjustified-evil argument, comparative evolutionary-evil argument, and heaven-model reply are logically distinct and contact separate burdens; merging any pair would erase either a different evidential method or a direct reply.

bridges.statement: The cumulative case and replies support the conclusion that God exists.
Change and concurrent dependence terminate in a first actualizer that is pure actuality.
The impossibility of an infinite past supports a finite beginning and divine cause of the universe.
Pure actuality entails the characteristic attributes of the God of classical theism.
God and pure actuality explain goodness, moral authority, equal human value, and responsibility.

routes.speaker: Ben Watkins
routes.position: Metaphysical naturalism: God does not exist

bridges.statement: On the total evidence, metaphysical naturalism is a better explanation than classical theism.
Naturalism has the higher prior probability because it is more modest and coherent.
Hiddenness, unjustified evil, and evolutionary suffering conflict with a perfect creator and favor naturalistic indifference.
Classical divine attributes generate internal tensions and do not follow from the cosmological conclusions.
Necessary, irreducibly normative moral truths explain moral reality without God and undermine the theistic moral inference.
